Its promise is immense - to decarbonize heavy industry, enable green industrialization, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security - yet its trajectory remains uncertain. How can green hydrogen truly become a development pathway?

Green hydrogen must serve sustainable development, not just markets. People must be at the center, with local value chains that create jobs and new industries. A priority of needs of the Planet must guide the use and preservation of water and land for long-term resilience. And Prosperity should be shared - with green hydrogen fueling industrialization, enhancing energy security, and decarbonizing growth.
 
Our new policy paper by UNDP  and TIDE Centre, University of Oxford , Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework, introduces this 3P approach - People, Planet, and Prosperity - to help countries steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction 👉 bit.ly/Green-H2

Green #hydrogen is projected to be able to reach 7-8% of final energy demand by 2050, more than double the needs of the entire shipping sector today.

But hydrogen must complement—never replace—development objectives.
 
At today’s #COP30 dialogue organized by the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition  and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , I steered the discussion to explore how to ensure green hydrogen supports national development priorities, protects ecosystems, and creates shared prosperity.

1️⃣ Align hydrogen with national development priorities:
When tied to national strategies, these investments can decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors and build local industry and energy security. Without this, they risk becoming extractive, with value exported and impacts retained.

2️⃣ Strengthen governance across the land–water–energy system
Hydrogen is not a standalone investment—it depends on water resources, land availability, and grid capacity. In Namibia, a 2-million-tonne project would require 18 million m³ of water annually, equivalent to the needs of more than 250,000 people. Countries need integrated planning, clear regulation, and national innovation systems.

3️⃣ Ensure hydrogen creates local prosperity, not only export pathways:
Not every country can or should pursue large-scale hydrogen. The right pathway depends on water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.  Where hydrogen is viable, it must deliver domestic value: but in local jobs, resilient value chains, and equitable benefits.

These priorities underpin the UNDP –TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  report “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen”, which introduces a People–Planet–Prosperity framework to help countries determine where hydrogen adds genuine value: 🔗📘 bit.ly/Green-H2
 
#GreenHydrogen #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SDG7 #COP30 COP30 Brazil

Global investments in the energy transition reached a new record of USD 2.4 trillion in 2024, a 20% increase compared to the previous year. But it’s not enough to achieve the global goal of tripling renewable capacity by 2030 and it remains highly concentrated in the most advanced economies. 

The facts:

➤ Renewable energy investment reached a new record too with USD 807 billion in 2024. But year-on-year annual growth slowed, with 7.3% in 2024 compared to 32% the year before.

➤ Investment in renewable power, grids and battery storage exceeded fossil fuels investment in 2024, but fossil spending is on the rise. 

➤ Investment in energy transition technologies grew globally, but 90% remained concentrated in advanced economies and China, leaving emerging and developing countries behind. 

As leaders meet at COP30 to advance the ‘Baku to Belém Roadmap to 1.3 trillion’, scaling finance for emerging and developing countries is essential to make the transition truly inclusive and global.

IRENA has long called for smarter use of public funds to unlock private investment through risk-mitigation tools. The Global Landscape of Energy Transition Finance 2025 (https://lnkd.in/dmx9uuUn), a new report by IRENA and the Climate Policy Initiative shows that advanced and major economies can draw on domestic financial resources to fund energy transitions.
 
In contrast, lower-income countries depend on external support due to underdeveloped financial markets, limited fiscal capacity, high capital costs, and debt vulnerabilities amongst others.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, and smart financing architectures.

The success of Africa’s energy transformation will not be measured by kilometres of cable laid, but by households switching on lights, health centres powering lifesaving equipment, and businesses growing with reliable, affordable electricity. Africa’s infrastructure is expanding fast—yet millions of connected households remain in the dark. Not only because the grid never reached them, but because they cannot afford to use it. 220 million Africans cannot afford basic electricity consumption, and 400 million cannot afford 500 kWh/year, barely a tenth of an average European household.

This affordability gap is one of the defining challenges for Africa’s economic future—but also a real opportunity to shape a new energy paradigm: one where investments are targeted, financing costs fall, and partnerships drive scalable, country-led solutions.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat, I reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to universal electrification in line with the UN-Energy Pledge. I had the pleasure to reflect with Aboubacar Said Anli, Minister of Energy, Water, and Hydrocarbons, #Comoros, Nialé Kaba, Minister of Minister of Planning and Development, #Côte d’Ivoire, Michael Franz , Team Leader, GET. Invest and moderated by Daniel Schroth Director at African Development Bank Group  , on how to ensure electricity is not only available but affordable, inclusive, and transformative:

1️⃣ Shift from counting connections to measuring development outcomes — in health, education, livelihoods, and productivity.
2️⃣ Reduce the cost of capital, which is 3–4 times higher in Africa; narrowing this gap can cut project costs by 15–25%.
3️⃣ Strengthen partnerships across governments, DFIs, development partners, and the private sector to align financing and delivery at scale.

This is where Mission 300 becomes catalytic. With coordinated compacts, unified delivery frameworks, and blended investment pipelines, #M300 shows how strategic partnerships can amplify impact, accelerate financing, and translate ambition into real improvements in people’s lives. UNDP stands with the The World Bank , AfDB, and all Mission 300 partners in transforming energy systems into engines of development, inclusion, and resilience.
Kevin KARIUKI The Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, and smart financing architectures.

The success of Africa’s energy transformation will not be measured by kilometres of cable laid, but by households switching on lights, health centres powering lifesaving equipment, and businesses growing with reliable, affordable electricity. Africa’s infrastructure is expanding fast—yet millions of connected households remain in the dark. Not only because the grid never reached them, but because they cannot afford to use it. 220 million Africans cannot afford basic electricity consumption, and 400 million cannot afford 500 kWh/year, barely a tenth of an average European household.

This affordability gap is one of the defining challenges for Africa’s economic future—but also a real opportunity to shape a new energy paradigm: one where investments are targeted, financing costs fall, and partnerships drive scalable, country-led solutions.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat, I reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to universal electrification in line with the UN-Energy Pledge. I had the pleasure to reflect with Aboubacar Said Anli, Minister of Energy, Water, and Hydrocarbons, #Comoros , Nialé Kaba, Minister of Minister of Planning and Development, #Côte d’Ivoire, Michael Franz , Team Leader, GET. Invest and moderated by Daniel Schroth Director at African Development Bank Group , on how to ensure electricity is not only available but affordable, inclusive, and transformative:

1️⃣ Shift from counting connections to measuring development outcomes — in health, education, livelihoods, and productivity.
2️⃣ Reduce the cost of capital, which is 3–4 times higher in Africa; narrowing this gap can cut project costs by 15–25%.
3️⃣ Strengthen partnerships across governments, DFIs, development partners, and the private sector to align financing and delivery at scale.

This is where Mission 300 becomes catalytic. With coordinated compacts, unified delivery frameworks, and blended investment pipelines, #M300 shows how strategic partnerships can amplify impact, accelerate financing, and translate ambition into real improvements in people’s lives. UNDP stands with the The World Bank , AfDB, and all Mission 300 partners in transforming energy systems into engines of development, inclusion, and resilience. Great week in Port Moresby, where I had the privilege of co-organising with the UNDP Papua New Guinea Country Office colleagues and National Energy Authority - NEA an international conference on Advancing Energy Access: PNG Mini-grid Policy and Implementation. 

The event marked the official validation of Papua New Guinea’s Off-grid Regulation for Small Power Systems.

This regulation is a strategic lever to accelerate energy access in one of the most geographically complex contexts in the world. It provides a national framework for licensing, compliance, quality standards, and consumer protection, all essential to scaling renewable and hybrid mini-grids.

Throughout the event, we brought together institutions from the national and provincial levels, utilities, the private sector, development partners, and technical experts. The goal: move beyond policy intent and into implementation design.

To support this, I also delivered a dedicated technical training to National Energy Authority - NEA staff on the regulation’s structure, licensing pathways, dispute resolution mechanisms, tariff implications, and operationalization scenarios, equipping the institution to lead its national rollout.

Across the sessions, several priorities emerged:
🔹 Formal adoption of the regulation before December is essential to preserve regulatory continuity and unlock investment.
 🔹 NEA–PPL–province coordination mechanisms must be institutionalised, with clear roles for inspection, compliance, and system planning.
 🔹 Provincial governments and local communities must be systematically engaged, including through awareness campaigns and co-design models.
 🔹 A transparent, rule-based tariff framework must be finalised to balance cost-reflectivity with affordability, especially for low-income households.
 🔹 Private sector interest is strong — but must be matched by stability, predictability, and bankable implementation conditions.

The conference was supported by the Japan - The Government of Japan through the #PacificGreenTransformation Project, which is also advancing decentralized solar solutions in Bougainville, including innovation hubs and a flagship 1 MW mini-grid in Buin.

Green hydrogen is often presented as a technological silver bullet — but for developing countries, its real question is deeper: will it expand human development or reproduce old inequalities?

In a new UNDP–TIDE Centre report, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen, we propose a 3P Framework — People, Planet, Prosperity — to help countries steer hydrogen strategies toward development outcomes rather than extractive models.

Here are three insights shaping the debate:

👥 People: Green hydrogen must expand energy access, strengthen electricity systems, and invest in skills so workers participate in the transition — not get displaced by it.

🌍 Planet: Land, water, biodiversity and minerals face real pressures. Safeguards must come first so hydrogen supports ecological resilience instead of undermining it.

💼 Prosperity: Countries should integrate hydrogen into industrial policy, create local value chains, and move gradually — learning from early adopters to avoid first-mover risks.

The promise is real: decarbonizing heavy industry, powering green industrialisation, and creating inclusive jobs. It depends on how we govern it.

A just energy transition is not simply a technological shift. It is a development strategy. — it is social policy, industrial policy, climate policy, and a development priority all at once. 

This week, I’m with @UNDP colleagues in Dakar, Senegal, alongside 20+ country offices, energy experts, financiers and development practitioners to focus on what matters most: turning clean energy into development outcomes. 

Africa holds the world’s greatest renewable potential — including 60% of global high-quality solar and nearly 8,000 GW of solar capacity — and 30% of critical mineral reserves, positioning the continent to lead the green industrial economy.

How can we re-think Africa’s economic transformation through a just energy transition? 

Three opportunities will define its transition:
 
1️⃣ First, Africa is becoming central to the global clean-energy economy, building on green industry. Africa can go behind producing clean power — it can also industrialize it, from agro-processing to e-mobility to mineral value chains. A transformation that could save 3.7 million lives every year. 

2️⃣  Second, de-risking is essential to unlock finance at scale. Africa needs USD 190–200 billion annually for energy investment, yet risk is perceived at 2–3× reality. Blended finance, guarantees, and policy reform can flip this equation and turn pipelines into projects. 

3️⃣  Third, digitalization and AI make this transformation even more powerful, as scaling energy access is an economic imperative, which can reduce technical and commercial losses by up to 20-30%. Access must move from pilots to performance — especially for clean cooking and for deploying digital innovations that boost efficiency and productive use. 

#Digital and #AI tools can lower costs, improve planning, and support de-risking — but they are enablers, not substitutes. Community engagement, local capacity, and strong institutions remain the backbone of a just energy transition, especially where digital ecosystems are still emerging. 

Energy is ultimately about people, jobs, and dignity. This week in Dakar, with UNDP  colleagues and partners across Africa, we are working to turn the continent’s renewable wealth into universal access, green industries, and inclusive growth.

Thanks to our partner WeGO, the City Future Readiness Index (CFRI) has been featured in Foreign Policy Magazine.

After the successful launch of CFRI 2925 on 19 November 2025, Foreign Policy published a full article on the index and report, underlining in particular that :

1️⃣ London has been named the world’s most future-ready city in 2025, recognized for its unique blend of financial dynamism, cultural vitality, and global reach.

2️⃣ It is closely followed by San Francisco in second place, hailed as a global digital trailblazer, and Boston in third, renowned as a world-class research hub.

3️⃣ The top 10 is rounded out by global hubs Paris (4th) and New York (5th); smart, sustainable European cities Copenhagen (6th), Zurich (7th), and Stockholm (8th); and Asian innovation leaders Singapore (9th) and Seoul (10th).

The article also mentions that the CFRI distinguishes itself from other city assessment indices through its innovative, dual-structure approach. Developed by Descartes Institute in parnership with WeGO, it overcomes the limitations of opinion-survey-based indices by utilizing hard city-level data. This method ensures independence, rigor, and adaptability as data quality and coverage evolve. The index is designed as an actionable tool to better inform stakeholder decisions.

A particular attention is granted in the article to the “Metropolis Paradox” explored ion the full FCRI Report. While large, wealthy cities successfully leverage smart technologies to offset the diseconomies of scale - such as mobility and safety challenge - the report warns of a widening urban divide, calling for technological innovation, particularly the deployment of AI, to accelerate progress in urban design and management.

Another distinguishing factor of the CFRI is that it defines cities not just as narrow, single administrative units but incorporates an understanding of cities also as larger metropolitan regions or major urban centers of strategic importance for better comparison of diverse urban systems. 

In this era of rapid transition, the very definition of urban competitiveness is being reshaped. Consequently, city branding and global visibility have become crucial for those aspiring to an international role. The report also notes that talent strategies must evolve from simple attraction to facilitating “brain circulation,” while cities are increasingly building durable comparative advantages based on their unique history, culture, and experience.

From Belém to Antalya: Anchoring Transformation in Our Shared History

Thirty years ago, I wrote my master's thesis on the vocabulary of power of Ibn Khaldun. I was captivated by how this 14th-century scholar theorized economic transformation and the conditions that enable societies to change.

I didn't expect those insights would resonate so deeply with the climate transformation challenge we face today.

Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406) is perhaps the most studied scholar from the medieval Islamic world—and for good reason. He theorized economic development and societal change four centuries before Adam Smith. While his work has roots in the Muslim world, where it resonates profoundly, his insights have become universal. His work itself is a bridge between civilizations—born in North Africa, writing about societies from the Mediterranean to the Horn of Africa, offering frameworks that transcend any single tradition.

At the heart of his theory is 'asabiyyah (عصبية)—a concept often translated as "social solidarity" or "group cohesion," but which carries deeper meaning: the internal force that enables collective transformation.

Ibn Khaldun's insight was profound: Transformation doesn't come from external pressure or imposed mandates. It emerges from internal cohesion channeled through legitimate authority and grounded in economic realities.

This wasn't abstract philosophy. Ibn Khaldun was theorizing how actual societies move from one economic model to another—and why some succeed while others fracture.

As I watch today's climate debates, I keep returning to his framework:
The scale of transformation we need—from fossil fuel economies to clean energy systems—is precisely the kind of civilizational-economic shift Ibn Khaldun analyzed. Not just technical change, but transformation of how societies produce, consume, and organize themselves.

At COP30 in Belém, President Lula spoke of mutirão—collective effort. As we move toward COP31 in Antalya—a city that has itself been a bridge between continents and cultures for millennia—I wonder if Ibn Khaldun's framework might help us think more clearly about the political economy of climate transformation.

After 22 years working in sustainable development and multilateralism, I'm convinced: we need better theories of transformation, not just better targets.

Perhaps some of that wisdom has been waiting in our libraries—across cultures and centuries—for us to rediscover.

What intellectual traditions inform your thinking on transformation?

These services help governments, utilities, regulators and investors optimize renewable energy planning and operations, strengthen infrastructure resilience, and support evidence-based decisions that accelerate the energy transition and improve energy security. #WMO also contributes to global initiatives, technical guidance, capacity building, climate-energy research, and multi-partner reports that integrate climate insights into energy strategies, especially for solar, wind and hydropower. 

This means better forecasting of wind and solar resources, improved understanding of climate impacts on energy demand and supply, and smarter investment decisions that de-risk renewable deployment.

The energy transition is no longer just about decarbonisation.

The 'Smart City' has been closely linked with #energy since the term was introduced. From smart energy meters, to the role of Big Data for energy and grid management. I've been getting more and more questions about what a 'smart' city looks like and wanted to re-share this article I co-authored with Calum Handforth  a while back. We argue that we need fewer 'smart' cities, and more 'smarter' cities. Smarter cities which:

* Put people at the heart of urban and technology planning and deployment. Not cities that try to retro-fit tech and energy projects and programmes around perceived citizen needs.
* Use a broad tech and innovation toolkit, and don’t just chase the latest innovation. For example, Big Data is important, but so too is the 'Thick Data' which helps us to learn more about energy consumers - or those that are energy-poor.
* Focus on outcomes, and not just the rollout of solutions - and, especially, we need ‘Smarter Cities’ which invest in the ‘connective tissue’ that creates meaningful urban spaces and places. We don’t want cities to just become ‘platforms’ of ‘use-cases’.

When writing this article, we were also inspired by the exciting and important opportunities for 'smart cities' in the Global North to learn from their counterparts in the Global South. 

And this is particularly relevant for energy, when so many innovations - including decentralised renewable energy, pay-as-you-go solar and other innovative business models, and frugal energy innovations - could be as relevant in New York as they are in New Delhi.

Over the last two days, I have been inspired by the conversations and pioneering work emerging from the IRENA Youth Forum 2026, which brings together 140 youth selected from over 26,000 applicants worldwide, convened by the International Renewable Energy Agency.

This year’s theme, “Youth Innovation and Digital Solutions: From AI to Access in Renewable Energy”, is especially fitting as the Forum is being hosted at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence. Holding these discussions in a space dedicated to cutting-edge AI research reinforces a central message of the Forum: that artificial intelligence is no longer peripheral to the energy transition, but increasingly central to how energy systems are planned, governed, and deployed, particularly in developing and vulnerable contexts.

‘AI for Sustainable Energy for Development’

One of the most compelling sessions was delivered by Riad Meddeb, who explored how artificial intelligence can be leveraged to accelerate energy access and system efficiency in development contexts. What resonated most was the emphasis on governance before scale: AI’s potential to optimize grids, forecast demand, and support planning is significant, but without transparent decision-making frameworks and inclusive data ecosystems, these tools risk deepening existing inequalities. The session underscored that innovation in energy must be accompanied by accountability, institutional capacity, and human-centred design.

‘Youth Local Voices: From Local to Global Advocacy’

Equally impactful was the session led by Aitana Ramírez de Arellano Santiago, which examined how youth can translate local energy and climate challenges into credible international advocacy. The discussion moved beyond storytelling into strategy, focusing on framing, evidence, and alignment with global policy processes. For many of us working in vulnerable or under-represented contexts, the key takeaway was that local lived experience is not a limitation; when strategically framed, it is a powerful entry point into global decision-making spaces.

‘Gender and Social Impact of Renewable Energy and the Energy Transition’

The workshop facilitated by MARIA FLOUDA and Racha Moukayed McClelland offered a critical reminder that the energy transition is not only technical, but profoundly social. Discussions on gender, equity, and social outcomes highlighted that renewable energy projects can either reinforce existing power structures or actively transform them, depending on who is included in planning, ownership, and benefit-sharing. For Small Island Developing States 🏝️, the energy transition is not just about reforming energy systems. It is about economic stability, climate resilience, and national sovereignty. With renewables now cheaper than fossil fuels across most island grids, clean energy is no longer a cost—it is the smartest macro-economic choice.

Many #SIDS import the vast majority of their energy through fossil fuels. Around 60% import at least 90% of their energy, and in countries like the Maldives, fuel imports absorb more than 10% of GDP, reaching up to 16% across SIDS in some years. This dependence exposes economies to price volatility, supply disruptions, and extreme weather.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly, I discussed how SIDS are not waiting to transition — they are already leading it. Out of necessity and innovation, they are building power systems designed for climate resilience, energy independence, and the water-energy-food nexus, from solar-powered desalination to resilient island microgrids.

The real bottleneck today is not technology — it is finance. What SIDS need are bankable investment pathways that combine concessional capital, guarantees, and risk-sharing instruments to crowd in private investors at scale. This is where digital# data and #AI become transformative: by improving demand forecasting, data transparency, grid management, and real-time performance tracking, they reduce uncertainty, lower the cost of capital, and turn small, fragmented projects into investable portfolios.

So the question is no longer whether SIDS should transition.
It is how fast we can align #finance, guarantees, and digital intelligence to unlock clean-energy investments that match their ambition — and their urgency.

#RisingUpForSIDS

The #AI era and the energy transition are advancing rapidly –– but unequally. 565 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack electricity, and 900 million rely on biomass. Whilst annual data center spending to fuel the AI boom could require investments up to USD 7 trillion by 2030.

But improving the alignment of these 21st century trends could lead to important impact. 

When planned together, digital infrastructure and AI-enabled innovation can anchor new renewable generation, create reliable offtake, and catalyze local innovation ecosystems. 

What does AI mean for development if it does not change how people access energy, cook, or economic opportunities? During a Ministerial Address at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, I delved into what development-centered and meaningful AI-energy alignment looks like: 

1️⃣ AI is accelerating renewable deployment by turning planning into precision delivery: AI-enabled forecasting, digital twins, and grid analytics improve dispatch accuracy by 20-30% and cut curtailment by 10-12%, enabling faster integration of wind and solar at scale.

2️⃣ Digital systems are converting efficiency gains into fiscal space for access and inclusion: Energy inefficiency still drives nearly 60% of global energy losses, costing developing economies up to USD 1.3 trillion by 2030. Even a 10% efficiency gain, enabled by AI-based demand management and predictive maintenance, can unlock billions in savings.

3️⃣ Livelihood creation through productive use of energy: When energy and digital transitions converge, they create jobs, incomes, and development. And as clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for economic transformation.

With this emerging technology, we have the opportunity to revolutionize our energy systems, but only if AI is deliberately aligned with access, affordability, and resilience, rather than layered onto existing inequalities.

The energy transition will not be driven by ambition alone—it will be shaped by whether we can turn global capital into real, investable clean-energy markets where energy demand, development needs, and climate goals intersect. 

In 2024, global investment in energy transition technologies reached a record $2.4 trillion, up 20% from 2023. Yet more than 90% of these flows went to China and advanced economies, even as fossil fuel subsidies remain at $1.1 trillion and external debt servicing reached $1.4 trillion, with 61 countries spending over 10% of public revenues just to cover interest payments.

At the UNDP  session today at the @IRENA Pavilion during #WFES2026, we focused on how to do exactly that, looking at the 3 financial solutions that unlock opportunity:

1️⃣ Strengthening local ownership and value chains is essential to turn renewable deployment into development. In regions such as North Africa, capacity is scaling rapidly, but external ownership and export-oriented models limit job creation, skills, and domestic value capture.

2️⃣ Using debt-smart and blended finance instruments can restore fiscal space for clean energy. In non-oil-producing MENA countries, debt-to-GDP ratios approaching 90% are crowding out public investment in energy, health, and education—making guarantees, concessional capital, and debt-linked climate finance critical.

3️⃣ De-risking and demand-anchoring mechanisms can lower the cost of capital. Today, renewable projects in high-risk markets face financing costs two to three times higher than in advanced economies, even though the technologies are the same.

These realities point to a simple truth: scaling clean energy without reforming financial systems will reproduce inequality. The future of a just transition lies in what we learn - and change - when capital is structured to reduce risk, retain value locally, and support inclusive investment, energy solutions become affordable, resilient, and scalable—making a just energy transition the engine for development pathways that are truly sustainable.

#EnergyForDevelopment #WFES2026 #DevelopmentFinance #Derisking

Clean cooking needs $8 billion a year to reach universal access – but we’re mobilizing barely a third of that. This isn’t just a funding gap. It’s a development failure.  

As I said early today: “We’re paying trillions of dollars to avoid spending billions." 

At what point do we stop calling this an “investment gap” when the cost of doing nothing is a thousand times higher? 

The numbers speak for themselves: 

➡️ $2.4 trillion – the estimated annual cost of dirty cooking in terms of healthcare, environmental degradation, and lost productivity. 

➡️ $2.5 billion - the total annual investment currently going into clean cooking solutions. That’s not even a third of what’s needed to achieve universal access by 2030. 

This is not an “investment gap.” It’s a missed opportunity to align climate, health, gender equity, and economic development goals through a single intervention. To change the trajectory, we need to shift the financing paradigm. Here are three catalytic approaches leading the way: 

1️⃣ Blended finance: Combining grants, guarantees, and concessional capital to de-risk private investment, reduce end-user costs, and help early-stage enterprises scale. 

2️⃣ Digital pay-as-you-go systems: Leveraging mobile payments and smart tech to improve affordability, enable real-time monitoring, and unlock access to carbon and impact finance. 

3️⃣ Outcome-based financing: Linking investor returns directly to measurable social and health results, shifting focus from inputs to verified impact. 

At UNDP, we’re advancing these models through Financial Innovation Labs, turning clean cooking from a development afterthought into core climate and infrastructure investment opportunities. Let’s de-risk, digitize, and diversify. Clean cooking is not a side issue; it's a frontline solution for sustainable development. #EnergyforDevelopment #CleanCooking

I really enjoyed recording this pod with my friend and colleague, Siddharth Singh . In it, we went through the three distinct phases of global energy demand over the last 50 years:

1) 1970s - 2000s: OECD dominance. In the mid-70s the OECD accounted for around 80% of global GDP. This was reflected in energy consumption skewed towards these richer countries, where the energy intensive materials needed for cities and industries were concentrated.

2) Early 2000s to the present day: The rise of China. In just three decades, China's urban population has grown by 600 million people. It has added 300 million cars to the road, built 37,000 km of highspeed rail (4x the entire European total), and used more cement in two years than the US did over the entirety of the 20th century. This needed A LOT of energy, propelling China right to the top of the energy consumption league. In the last decade alone, China accounted for more than half of global oil and gas demand growth and 60 of electricity demand growth. 

3) The future: China's working age population, its cement production and its steel output have all peaked. In the next 20 years, India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America could add 3x times the number of people to their urban populations as China did over the last decade. Rising wealth, access rates, and demand for services like cooling and water desalination that are exacerbated by rising temperatures and climate change, will all lead to a further shift in the geography of global energy demand.

We are now in the #Zettabyte era - generating volumes of data never seen before in human history. With just one zettabyte equivalent to a trillion gigabytes, we often hear data being called the the new oil, gold, or currency. But data only creates value when it is translated into decisions. 

Data centres already consume 1.5–2% of global electricity, rising to 5–20% in major digital hubs, while putting growing pressure on power systems, water, and land. 

At the same time, when the just energy transition and the digital revolution are planned together, clean power and data reinforce each other. When clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for jobs, livelihoods, and sustainable development — not just electrons.

This is why, at UNDP , we are working closely with governments and energy partners to turn data into a development asset for the AI and energy transition. Earlier today, at #WFES2026 we reflected on what we are learning in practice. 
Three strategic insights stand out:

1️⃣Data, digital and AI are now a core asset for clean energy investment and delivery. High-quality energy data can de-risk projects and attract capital — but only if digital energy systems are cyber-secure. As grids become digital, cybersecurity becomes energy security, protecting hospitals, water systems, and local businesses. Geospatial and context-specific data can significantly improve energy planning, identify viable investments, and accelerate rollout.

2️⃣ Focus must shift from data systems to data ecosystems. Energy solutions increasingly generate data, but transformational impact depends on how these data flow across institutions, sectors and stakeholders. Building inclusive energy ecosystems requires systems-level approaches; linking data, energy priorities and development objectives, from national policy to local delivery.	

3️⃣ Data transparency and accountability can make energy systems inclusive. Our data shows 447 million “electrified” people do not actually use power. When energy data is transparent and well-governed, utilities and investors become accountable for who is served and who is left behind — turning energy systems into platforms for livelihoods and inclusive development, not just grid connections.

As we move deeper into the AI and energy transition, the real challenge is not generating more data - but using it effectively and governing it better, together. The future of the energy transition will be shaped not by how much data we generate, but on whether data systems reflect lived realities, enable better decisions, and align digital innovation with equitable energy outcomes

#EnergyForDevelopment #DataGovernance #WEFS #ThickData #BigData

Green hydrogen: fuel of the future, or risking another development divide?
 
Green hydrogen is a potential catalyst of sustainable development. Producing hydrogen through 100% renewable electricity could significantly reduce emissions, whilst also powering the sectors, industries, and opportunities that drive countries' growth and development. Green hydrogen could decarbonise heavy industry, support green industrialisation, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security.
 
It has the potential to supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050.
 
But, how can we maximise its benefits - whilst avoiding creating, or entrenching, a new energy and technology divide?
 
1️⃣ Green hydrogen is not for everyone
As with other energy solutions, green hydrogen is one tool in the sustainable energy toolkit. Not every country is suited for large-scale hydrogen. Water availability, energy access needs, land use, and national development priorities must guide decisions. National leaders, and energy agencies, need to be supported and empowered to build the renewable energy portfolios that make sense for their local context.
 
2️⃣Take a holistic approach to energy planning, and don't undermine national climate priorities
Scaling hydrogen is resource-intensive, placing real pressure on land, water, and power systems. 2 million tonnes alone requires around 18 million cubic metres of water, making value creation highly sensitive to how projects are planned and governed. Hydrogen deployment needs to align with climate goals and with the responsible use of water and land. If these are in sync, the potential is considerable. .
 
3️⃣ Green hydrogen needs to deliver domestic value, and people need to come first
Jobs, skills, and local supply chains do not emerge by themselves. Domestic value capture needs to be built into project design from the outset - reaffirming the need to ensure green hydrogen is relevant to national contexts. Similarly, communities benefit only when institutions, regulation, and investment frameworks are aligned to protect resources and distribute gains fairly. Green energy needs to support people, and not just markets.
 
The potential of green hydrogen is immense. In South Africa alone, projections suggest a 3.6% increase in GDP and 370,000 new jobs by 2050. But these outcomes are not inevitable. Green hydrogen can be a powerful development accelerator. But only if it is designed intentionally to strengthen resilience, build local value, and support inclusive growth.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen

Energy has been centre stage at #Davos this week. And, amid all of this: AI. AI is not artificial. It has a long tail of energy-hungry physical data centres and GPU racks, critical mineral mining, and real-world inference demanding unprecedented power supplies.

So, how do we harness these two seemingly separate but, in reality, interconnected and intertwined revolutions - the energy transition, and the AI era? This is the focus of our new Bulletin, below, where we define the ‘digital energy stack’.

In the tech world, a ’stack’ is the collection of different technologies and components needed for a digital product or service to function. As you read this post, it sits on a ’stack’ of solutions: a web browser or LinkedIn application on your phone or other device. Internet and email protocols that (hopefully!) are displaying the below graphic and link correctly. And, layers of cloud hosting, connectivity, and - of course - energy, to make all of this happen.

We are applying this ‘stack’ approach to sustainable energy. We need a systems-level approach, and coherent and strategic efforts. There are seven elements in the ’digital energy stack’:

📊 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 - the 'fuel' of the energy revolution. Big, Lean, and Thick Data.
📱 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 - including 3G and 4G, and IoT.
🖥️ 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞 - the 'currency' of the 21st century.
🪪 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 - to amplify the impact of inclusive energy.
🔒 𝐂𝐲𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 - recognising energy's status as critical national infrastructure. 
🤖 𝐀𝐈 - with AI driving new energy solutions, but also creating new challenges.
🏛️ 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 - shaping the talent, culture, and  institutions of the energy transition.

Importantly, there is no single pathway for any of these seven components. Digital and energy innovation is occurring and emerging everywhere, from Silicon Valley to the Silicon Savannah. The Global South is not just an innovation taker - but a maker, and shaper.

Without intentional design, digital risks reinforcing and entrenching energy inequality rather than accelerating an inclusive and just energy transition. The question is no longer whether AI and energy will intersect. It is whether we design that intersection to deliver development, resilience, and equity at scale.

We invite partners, policymakers, and practitioners to help shape the digital energy stack with us 👉https://lnkd.in/eYRYQnmu

#EnergyForDevelopment #AI #DigitalEnergyStack
